source_text: Pugnasse quidem cum principe tenebrarum deum lucis, Manichaeus finxit, et credidit, addiditque eius captivam teneri in hoc orbe substantiam; sed tantam infelicitatem colore pietatis nititur excusare, affirmans eum quasi bonum pro patria dimicasse civem, atque ideo obiecisse membra, ne perderet regna. Tu qui haec didiceras, quantum ea vel ad tempus deserendo profeceris intuere; dicis, Deum necessitatem non pertulisse belli, sed iniquitatem admisisse iudicii; nec tenebrosis hostibus, sed perspicuis subiacere criminibus; non impertisse postremo substantiam suam, sed aeternam violasse iustitiam. Quo quis vestrum peior sit, aliis aestimandum relinquo. Illud tamen liquet, ad unum vos opinionis nefas redire. Nam et Manichaeus subscribit iniquitatem Deo suo, cum eum allegat damnaturum, in ultimo die membra quae tradidit; et tu per hoc illum asseris infelicem, per quod corrumpit gloriam qua cluebat, et persequendo innocentiam quam creavit, perdidit iustitiam qua sacerrimus fuit. Tantum igitur huic, quem tu inducis Deo ille, quem magister tuus commentus fuerat, antecellit, quantum excusabilius est praelio superatum esse quam vitio.
pass_a_gloss: That the god of light fought with the prince of darkness, the Manichaean invented, and believed, and added that his captive substance is held in this globe; but he strives to excuse so great an unhappiness with a color of piety, affirming that he fought as if a good citizen for the fatherland, and therefore threw his members in the way, lest he lose kingdoms. You who had learned these things, look how much you have profited by deserting them even for a time; you say that God did not bear a necessity of war, but admitted an iniquity of judgment; and that he is subject not to dark enemies but to clear crimes; finally that he did not impart his own substance, but violated eternal justice. Which of you is worse, I leave to others to estimate. That nevertheless is liquid, that you return to one crime of opinion. For both the Manichaean subscribes iniquity to his own god, when he alleges that he will condemn, on the last day, the members which he handed over; and you through this assert him unhappy, through this that he corrupts the glory in which he was famed, and by persecuting the innocence which he created, has lost the justice by which he was most sacred. So much therefore that one whom your teacher had invented surpasses this God whom you bring in, as it is more excusable to have been overcome in battle than by vice.

pass_b_english: The Manichaean invented and believed that the god of light fought with the prince of darkness; he added that this god's substance is held captive in this world. But he tries to excuse so great a misfortune under an appearance of piety, asserting that his god fought like a good citizen for his homeland and exposed his limbs to danger rather than lose his kingdom. You learned these things. Consider how much progress you made by abandoning them, even for a time! You say that God was not forced to undergo war but committed an unjust judgment; that he is not subject to dark enemies but to plainly evident crimes; and finally that he did not part with his own substance but violated eternal justice. I leave others to judge which of you is worse. This much is clear: you arrive at one and the same wicked opinion. The Manichaean assigns injustice to his god when he says that on the last day his god will condemn the members he himself surrendered. You too declare God miserable, because he ruins the glory that made him renowned and, by persecuting the innocence he created, loses the justice that made him supremely holy. The god your teacher invented therefore surpasses the God you introduce by just as much as defeat in battle is more excusable than defeat by vice.
